questions.stem: A PC suddenly cannot access the network or browse the internet. Why might malware deliberately cause this?

choices.text: To block you from downloading antivirus updates or removal tools

questions.explanation: Modern malware often cuts your network lifeline to stop you from downloading antivirus updates or removal tools - like locking the driveway so you can't go get help.
questions.trap: It's a deliberate self-defense tactic by the malware, not a performance or power-saving feature.

questions.stem: When malware blocks internet access so you can't download removal tools, what is a recommended way to clean the system?

choices.text: Boot from external media to clean the system
Wait for the malware to remove itself

questions.explanation: When malware blocks internet access, you may need to boot from external media to clean the system from outside the infected OS.
questions.trap: Disabling antivirus or waiting does nothing; booting from trusted external media bypasses the malware's blocks.

questions.stem: A desktop alert screams that your antivirus has expired or that you have a thousand viruses, urging you to call a number or click a link. What is this, and what should you do?

choices.text: A legitimate Windows alert; call the number immediately
Scareware; do not click it and instead run a scan with your own trusted software
A driver update; install it right away
A Windows Update notification; restart now

questions.explanation: These are scareware - false alerts designed to panic you into calling a scam number or clicking a malicious link. Don't click them; run a legitimate scan with your own trusted software.
questions.trap: These pop-ups are a fake emergency 'production,' not a real system alert - never call the number or click the link.

questions.stem: System files are suddenly renamed or missing, and you're denied access to your own documents. What does this likely indicate?
questions.explanation: Renamed or missing system files and sudden denial of access to your own documents are signs of a serious malware breach.
questions.trap: A routine Windows update does not rename your files or lock you out of your own documents.

questions.stem: Windows Update keeps failing. Besides Windows itself, what should you check first, given malware often targets the update service?
questions.explanation: Malware often blocks the update service to keep security holes open, so if updates act up, check connectivity and firewall settings first.
questions.trap: Resolution, wallpaper, and fonts have nothing to do with the update service being blocked.

questions.stem: You're seeing frequent random pop-ups even with the pop-up blocker enabled. What do you most likely have?
questions.explanation: Frequent random pop-ups despite an enabled pop-up blocker most likely mean adware is installed.
questions.trap: Power supply and CMOS battery issues cause hardware symptoms, not browser pop-ups.

questions.stem: You type a search or web address but the browser forcibly sends you to a different, shady site. What is this a classic sign of?
questions.explanation: Browser redirection - being forcibly sent to a different, often shady site - is a classic sign of a browser hijacker.
questions.trap: A weak Wi-Fi signal slows browsing but doesn't redirect you to specific malicious sites.

questions.stem: A browser shows a certificate warning ('your connection is not private'). Before assuming an attack, what simple local setting should you check first?
questions.explanation: An incorrect system date/time makes the computer think a certificate is expired or not yet valid, triggering a false certificate warning - check it before panicking.
questions.trap: Theme, mouse sensitivity, and tab count have nothing to do with certificate validation.

questions.stem: A browser is sluggish and CPU usage is pinned at 100% while on a website. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: A malicious website running a cryptominer in the background
The monitor refresh rate is too low

questions.explanation: A browser pinned at 100% CPU on a site can mean a malicious website is running a cryptominer in the background, using your hardware to make money for criminals.
questions.trap: Bookmarks and monitor refresh rate don't drive CPU to 100%; a cryptominer does.

questions.stem: Which response to a fake 'scareware' antivirus alert is correct?

choices.text: Call the phone number shown in the alert
Click the alert to renew your antivirus
Ignore it and run a scan only with your own installed, trusted antivirus
Forward the alert to all contacts

questions.explanation: Ignore fake scareware alerts and trust only your own installed antivirus to run a legitimate scan.
questions.trap: Calling the number or clicking the alert is exactly what the scam wants - it leads to more malware or a scam.
